nodes.name: test_context.rs
nodes.summary: Implements TestAppContext and VisualTestContext, the low-level test contexts that dispatch actions/keystrokes, await conditions, capture notifications and events, and drive rendering deterministically.
nodes.languageNotes: run_until_parked plus a controllable dispatcher gives deterministic async test execution; condition/next_event helpers let tests await entity state and emitted events.

nodes.name: visual_test_context.rs
nodes.summary: Defines VisualTestAppContext for offscreen visual tests: opens real offscreen windows, simulates full input, waits for animations, and captures screenshots for pixel-level verification.

nodes.name: binding.rs
nodes.summary: Defines KeyBinding, which pairs a keystroke sequence with an action and optional context predicate, and matches typed keystrokes against bindings.

nodes.name: context.rs
nodes.summary: Implements KeyContext and the KeyBindingContextPredicate parser/evaluator that scopes keybindings to UI contexts via a boolean expression language (and/or/child/eq).

nodes.name: app_menu.rs

nodes.name: bench_dispatcher.rs

nodes.name: AsyncWindowContext

nodes.name: Context

nodes.name: spawn_in

nodes.name: EntityMap
nodes.summary: Slot-based storage for all app entities, handling reservation, insertion, leasing for exclusive access, reference counting, and reclamation of dropped entities.

nodes.name: AnyEntity

nodes.name: Entity

nodes.name: AnyWeakEntity

nodes.name: WeakEntity
nodes.summary: Typed weak handle to an entity of type T that upgrades to a strong Entity and supports read/update through a context.

nodes.name: LeakDetector
nodes.summary: Diagnostic tool that records handle creation/release with backtraces and asserts no new entity leaks between snapshots.

nodes.name: HeadlessAppContext
nodes.summary: Runs a GPUI app without a physical display, supporting offscreen window opening, screenshot capture, controlled clock advancement, and parking control.

nodes.name: TestApp

nodes.name: TestAppContext

nodes.name: VisualTestContext

nodes.name: parse_expr

nodes.summary: Drives all pending main-thread tasks and due timers to completion, returning when the dispatcher reaches an idle state.

nodes.summary: A keystroke as it appears in a keybinding, wrapping an inner Keystroke with a platform keyboard mapper so bindings can be matched against and rendered per layout.

nodes.name: Modifiers

nodes.name: parse
nodes.summary: Parses a textual keystroke specification (e.g. "cmd-shift-p") into a Keystroke, resolving modifier tokens and the terminal key while rejecting malformed input.

nodes.name: should_match
nodes.summary: Determines whether one keystroke should match another for keybinding dispatch, accounting for modifier and key-char equivalence.

nodes.name: is_printable_key

nodes.name: LineLayout

nodes.name: compute_wrap_boundaries
nodes.summary: Computes soft-wrap break points for a shaped line given a wrap width, respecting word boundaries and glyph advances.

nodes.name: _index_for_position
nodes.summary: Maps a pixel position within a wrapped line back to the nearest text index, used for cursor placement and hit-testing.

nodes.name: layout_line_by_hash
nodes.summary: Shapes a line and stores it in the cache keyed by content hash so identical lines are reused across frames.

nodes.name: layout_wrapped_line

nodes.name: line_wrapper.rs

nodes.name: LineWrapper
nodes.summary: Wraps and truncates lines of text against a width budget, producing wrap boundaries and ellipsized runs.

nodes.name: truncate_wrapped_line

nodes.name: should_truncate_line_middle
nodes.summary: Decides whether and where to apply middle truncation, preserving the start and end of the text around an ellipsis.

nodes.name: paint_line_background
nodes.summary: Paints the background highlights behind a line's decoration runs before the glyphs are drawn.

nodes.name: to_json

nodes.name: connection.rs
nodes.summary: Implements the core proxy connection handling for the sandbox HTTP proxy: parses raw client requests (CONNECT/absolute-form/origin-form), enforces an allowlist and private-IP denial policy, resolves routes (direct or via an upstream proxy), and pumps bytes bidirectionally between client and destination sockets.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a hand-rolled HTTP/1.1 request parser (httparse) plus manual socket plumbing and a Route/RouteFailure enum to separate policy decisions from I/O.

nodes.name: ClientStream
nodes.summary: Enum wrapping either a TCP or Unix-domain client stream, implementing a uniform read/write/shutdown interface for the proxy's client connection handling.

nodes.name: StreamIo
nodes.summary: Trait-like abstraction providing a shutdown method over different stream types used by the proxy.

nodes.name: ParsedRequest
nodes.summary: Enum representing a parsed client HTTP request, distinguishing CONNECT tunnel requests from ordinary HTTP forward requests, with a parse method that normalizes absolute-form and authority-form targets.

nodes.name: Route
nodes.summary: Enum describing how a destination should be reached: directly or via a configured upstream proxy.

nodes.name: RouteFailure
nodes.summary: Enum describing why route planning failed, distinguishing policy denial from resolution/connection errors so callers can respond appropriately.

nodes.name: handle
nodes.summary: Top-level entry point for handling one client connection: reads request headers, parses the request, and dispatches to CONNECT or HTTP-forward handling.

nodes.name: read_request_headers
nodes.summary: Reads bytes from the client socket incrementally until a complete HTTP header block (double CRLF) is found.

nodes.name: build_origin_form_request
nodes.summary: Rewrites an absolute-form or authority-form proxy request into origin-form bytes suitable for forwarding to the destination server, stripping hop-by-hop proxy headers.

nodes.name: policy_denial
nodes.summary: Checks a requested host/port against the proxy's allowlist policy, returning a denial reason when the destination is not permitted.

nodes.name: plan_route
nodes.summary: Resolves a host/port to a concrete route, either via a configured upstream proxy or by direct DNS resolution filtered against forbidden (private/loopback) IPs.

nodes.name: is_forbidden_ip
nodes.summary: Determines whether an IP address is a loopback, private, or otherwise sandboxed-forbidden address, with an environment-variable escape hatch.

nodes.name: handle_connect
nodes.summary: Handles a CONNECT tunnel request end-to-end: enforces policy, opens a route to the destination, replies to the client, and pumps bytes bidirectionally until the tunnel closes.

nodes.name: handle_http_forward
nodes.summary: Handles a plain (non-CONNECT) HTTP forward request: enforces policy, opens a route, forwards the request bytes, and pumps the response back to the client.

nodes.name: miniprofiler_ui.rs
nodes.summary: GPUI-based in-app performance profiler window that polls the profiler crate's timing collector, merges timing samples across threads, and renders a live timeline including a remote-source mode for polling timings over a proto client connection.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a k-way merge to combine sorted per-thread timing streams and supports both local in-process collection and remote polling via a proto client, unified behind the same ProfilerWindow render path.

nodes.name: ProfileSource
nodes.summary: Enum describing where profiling data is sourced from: local foreground/all-threads or remote foreground/all-threads.

nodes.name: PerformanceProfilerSettings
nodes.summary: Settings struct holding whether the performance profiler feature is enabled, derived from the instrumentation settings content.

nodes.name: ProfilerWindow
nodes.summary: GPUI view that owns the profiler timing collector state, polling loop, remote polling task, and renders the live timeline UI including the source dropdown and per-thread timing bars.

nodes.name: init
nodes.summary: Registers the performance profiler feature: observes settings changes to toggle tracing and the command palette filter, and registers the workspace action to open the profiler window.

nodes.name: open_performance_profiler
nodes.summary: Opens the profiler window, focusing an existing window if one is already open for the workspace, or creating a new one otherwise.

nodes.name: new
nodes.summary: Constructs a ProfilerWindow, initializing timing collector state and polling task.

nodes.name: poll_timings
nodes.summary: Pulls new timing deltas from the collector or remote source and triggers a display timings rebuild.

nodes.name: rebuild_display_timings
nodes.summary: Recomputes the filtered, windowed set of timing bars to display based on autoscroll state and include-self-timings toggle.

nodes.name: set_source
nodes.summary: Switches the active profiling data source between local and remote modes and resets collected state.

nodes.name: start_remote_polling
nodes.summary: Spawns a background task that periodically requests timing snapshots over the remote proto client and applies the responses.

nodes.name: apply_remote_response
nodes.summary: Merges a remote profiling response's timing deltas into the local per-thread timing buffers.

nodes.name: render_source_dropdown
nodes.summary: Renders the dropdown UI element for switching between profiling source modes.

nodes.name: render_timing
nodes.summary: Renders a single timing bar element positioned and sized according to its start/duration within the visible window.

nodes.name: render
nodes.summary: Top-level render implementation for ProfilerWindow, laying out the toolbar, source dropdown, and the scrollable per-thread timeline.

nodes.name: kway_merge
nodes.summary: Merges multiple sorted lists of timing samples into a single sorted list using a k-way merge algorithm.

nodes.name: append_to_thread
nodes.summary: Appends new timing samples to the buffer for a given thread, creating the thread's entry if it does not yet exist.

layers.name: Application Entry & Distribution
layers.description: The zed application binary and CLI entry points plus lifecycle concerns — auto-update, crash reporting, session state, release channels, Windows packaging resources, and the bundled runtime assets (keymaps, themes, default settings, prompts, sounds) embedded into the app.

layers.name: GPUI Framework & Platform
layers.description: Zed's in-house GPU-accelerated UI framework (gpui) with its per-platform backends (Windows, macOS, Linux, web, wgpu), proc macros, async scheduler, media integration, and framework-level diagnostics like the element inspector and profiler UIs.

layers.name: Foundation & System Utilities
layers.description: Low-level shared infrastructure every other layer builds on: util/collections primitives, filesystem access, SQLite persistence (sqlez, db), HTTP clients and proxying, credentials and OAuth, logging/tracing/telemetry, feature flags, fuzzy matching, and sandboxing.

layers.name: Editor & Text Engine
layers.description: The core text-editing stack: the CRDT-backed text engine (text, rope, sum_tree, clock-free buffers), multi-buffer and diff handling, the editor view itself, Vim emulation, buffer/project search, and outline/go-to-line navigation.

layers.name: Language Intelligence
layers.description: Syntax and semantic language support: tree-sitter grammars, per-language configurations, LSP client, formatting via Prettier, the Node runtime host, snippets, and the bundled language extensions (GLSL, HTML, Protobuf, test fixtures).

layers.name: Project & Platform Services
layers.description: Headless workspace services that model the open project: project/worktree state, settings system and schema/migration tooling, tasks, terminal backend, Git integration, debug adapters (DAP), remote/dev-container connectivity, and the extension host and API.

layers.name: Workspace Shell & Feature UI
layers.description: The workspace window shell (panes, docks, panels) plus the reusable ui component library, theming, and all end-user feature UIs — file finder, project/outline panels, terminal and Git views, debugger UI, Jupyter REPL, markdown/SVG/CSV previews, settings and keymap editors, and onboarding.

layers.name: Collaboration & Cloud
layers.description: Multiplayer and cloud connectivity: the collab server with its Postgres migrations and k8s manifests, the RPC/proto wire protocol, the client connection layer, channels, calls with LiveKit audio, notifications, and cloud API types.

layers.name: AI & Agents
layers.description: The AI/agent stack retained for the note-taking app: the agent runtime and its UI, ACP threads, MCP context servers, prompt store, the language-model abstraction with a dozen provider integrations (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, Bedrock, …), Copilot, edit prediction (Zeta), web search, and eval harnesses.

layers.name: Build, CI & Project Support
layers.description: Everything that builds, ships, and documents the project: GitHub Actions workflows, ci/nix/script build and packaging automation, cargo/xtask/lint tooling, Dockerfiles and root configuration, benchmarks, legal notices, and repository-level docs and agent instructions.

layers.name: Bundled Language Extensions
layers.description: First-party language extensions shipped in the extensions/ directory (GLSL, HTML, protobuf, plus the test extension): extension manifests, tree-sitter query files, and LSP adapter code. Removal candidates for the note-taking fork.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README and contributor guide to orient yourself: this codebase is Zed, a GPU-accelerated multiplayer code editor written almost entirely in Rust, which you are forking into an academic note-taking and paper-writing app. The workspace contains roughly 250 crates under crates/, and CONTRIBUTING.md includes a bird's-eye view of how upstream organizes the code. Keep the fork's goal in mind throughout the tour: markdown/LaTeX/Jupyter workflows stay central, while collaboration, debugger, and extension machinery are candidates for removal.

tour.title: Application Entry Point
tour.description: Everything launches from crates/zed: main.rs parses CLI arguments, initializes the GPUI application, and sets up crash handling, paths, and fonts, then hands off to zed.rs, the wiring hub that initializes global state, registers application-level actions, and builds windows. The crate's Cargo.toml shows the full dependency fan-out — nearly every other crate in the workspace is pulled in here, making this the map of what your app actually ships. When you remove features (debugger, remote dev, extensions), this is where they get unplugged.
tour.languageLesson: Rust binaries live in a crate with a main.rs, while reusable logic goes in lib-style modules. Zed splits these: main.rs is a thin bootstrap, and zed.rs is the library that composes the app — a common pattern that keeps the binary testable.

tour.title: GPUI: The In-House UI Framework
tour.description: Zed does not use a web view or an off-the-shelf toolkit — it renders with GPUI, its own GPU-accelerated framework, and every panel or view you will build for the notebook app is a GPUI entity. The crate root re-exports the public API and defines the context traits, while app.rs is the heart: the App owns all entities, windows, and globals, and drives an effect queue that propagates notifications. Read the GPUI README first for the mental model; understanding entities, contexts, and the ownership model is the single biggest prerequisite for modifying this codebase.

tour.title: GPUI: Windows, Elements, and the Render Loop
tour.description: Building on Step 3's App, window.rs orchestrates the per-window draw loop — layout, prepaint, and paint passes plus focus, hitbox, and input dispatch — while element.rs defines the Element/IntoElement/Render traits that every visual component implements. GPUI is immediate-mode-flavored: each frame, your Render implementation returns a new element tree, which the framework lays out and paints. Your infinite-canvas whiteboard would live here as a custom Element with its own layout and paint logic.
tour.languageLesson: GPUI leans heavily on Rust traits as interfaces: Render is what makes a struct a view, and IntoElement lets heterogeneous components compose into one tree. The AnyElement type-erased wrapper is the Rust equivalent of dynamic dispatch over a closed lifecycle (request_layout -> prepaint -> paint).

tour.title: The Text Engine: SumTree, Rope, CRDT Buffer
tour.description: Underneath every open note is a three-layer text stack. SumTree is a persistent B-tree annotated with associative summaries — the workhorse data structure used across the whole codebase for text, file trees, and diffs. Rope stores UTF-8 text as a SumTree of chunks so edits and coordinate conversions are logarithmic, and text.rs layers a CRDT on top: Buffer stores fragments with Lamport timestamps so concurrent edits merge deterministically. Even in a single-user notebook app the CRDT stays — it is what powers undo history and the AI agent's concurrent edits.
tour.languageLesson: SumTree is a persistent (immutable, structurally-shared) data structure: cloning a snapshot is cheap because unchanged subtrees are shared via Arc. This is why Zed can hand immutable BufferSnapshots to background threads without locking.

tour.title: Language-Aware Buffers
tour.description: The language crate wraps the raw CRDT buffer from Step 5 with everything language-aware: buffer.rs defines the collaborative Buffer that layers tree-sitter syntax parsing, diagnostics, and git diff state onto text edits, and language.rs defines the Language type — grammar, tree-sitter queries, config, and LSP adapters. This is where markdown and LaTeX support plug in: each language is a bundle of a grammar plus query files, so improving LaTeX editing means working with these types.

tour.title: The Editor View
tour.description: editor.rs is the largest and most connected file in the codebase (highest fan-out, 48 imports): the Editor entity ties buffers, selections, LSP features, and rendering into the text-editing surface users actually type in. Two supporting pieces matter: multi_buffer.rs stitches several buffers into one virtually-contiguous surface (used for search results and diffs), and display_map.rs maps buffer coordinates to screen coordinates through layered transforms — folds, inlays, tab expansion, soft wrap. element.rs is the GPUI Element from Step 4 that actually paints lines, cursors, and the gutter. Any inline rendering you add (LaTeX equations, embedded media) flows through the display map and this element.

tour.title: Project, Worktrees, and Buffers on Disk
tour.description: Above individual buffers sits the Project entity, which composes every headless service: buffer management, worktrees, LSP, git, tasks, and search. A worktree models one root folder as an in-memory snapshot (again a SumTree of entries) kept fresh by a background filesystem scanner; worktree_store.rs manages the set of open roots and buffer_store.rs manages the lifecycle of open buffers — opening, saving, reloading. For a notes app, Project is effectively 'the open notebook or research folder', and this layer is where file organization features would live.

tour.title: Workspace Shell: Panes, Docks, Panels
tour.description: The workspace crate is the window chrome around everything from Steps 7-8: Workspace is the root view coordinating the center pane group, docks, toolbar, and modal layers. A Pane is a tabbed container holding Items (an editor, a terminal, a markdown preview), and Dock plus the Panel trait define the left/right/bottom side panels. To add a new surface to the app — an audio-memo panel or a whiteboard tab — you implement the Item or Panel trait and register it here, which is why this crate ranks near the top in fan-out.

tour.title: Design System, Themes, and Settings
tour.description: Three crates give the app its consistent look and configurability. The ui crate is the reusable component library (buttons, lists, popovers) every feature UI builds from; theme defines Theme/ThemeFamily and the global appearance state; and settings registers the layered settings system on startup. The master default settings file in assets defines every built-in configuration key and is embedded into the binary — when you add settings for your note-taking features, they get a schema entry here.
tour.languageLesson: Zed's settings use Serde-driven layered JSON: embedded defaults, then user, then project settings deserialize and merge into typed Rust structs. Adding a setting means defining a struct that derives Deserialize/JsonSchema, which also generates editor autocomplete for the settings file.

tour.title: Note-Taking Core: Markdown and Jupyter REPL
tour.description: These are the crates closest to your product vision. markdown.rs defines the Markdown GPUI entity that owns parse state and renders rich text (used throughout the UI, including agent chat), while markdown_preview is the side-by-side preview feature with its scroll-sync actions. The repl crate is the existing Jupyter integration: kernels/mod.rs defines the RunningKernel trait and KernelSpecification, and repl.rs wires sessions, kernels, and the ReplStore into the editor so code blocks execute inline. Extending these — better markdown editing, LaTeX rendering, richer notebook cells — is the heart of the fork.

tour.title: The AI and Agent Stack (Kept)
tour.description: The AI stack you are keeping has a clean two-tier design. language_model defines the abstract LanguageModel/LanguageModelProvider traits, and language_models registers a dozen concrete providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, Bedrock, ...) against that abstraction. On top, agent.rs implements the native ACP-compatible agent runtime — threads, tool calls, permissions — and agent_ui is its chat panel and thread UI in the workspace. For research workflows, this is where paper-summarization or citation tools would be added as agent tools.

tour.title: Foundation: Filesystem, Persistence, Terminal
tour.description: Beneath everything sit the foundation crates that most features depend on. fs.rs defines the Fs trait with a RealFs implementation and a fake for tests — all file I/O goes through it, which is what makes the codebase so testable. db.rs opens and migrates the local SQLite database (built on the sqlez wrapper, one of the graph's tightest clusters) that persists window state, sessions, and feature data — a natural home for note metadata. The terminal crates (model plus workspace Item view) are staying in your fork and are a good worked example of the model/view split used everywhere.

tour.title: Workspace Manifest and CI
tour.description: Finish with how the project builds and ships. The root Cargo.toml is the workspace manifest listing all ~250 member crates and shared dependency versions — when you delete a feature crate, it comes out of this file, and workspace-level lints and profiles are set here too. The run_tests workflow is the main CI gate upstream uses; as a solo fork you will likely prune the release automation but keep a slimmed test workflow. With this, you have the full loop: entry point, framework, text engine, editor, project, shell, features, and build.
tour.languageLesson: A Cargo workspace shares one Cargo.lock and target/ directory across all member crates, so cross-crate changes compile incrementally. workspace.dependencies centralizes version pins — individual crates reference them with `dep.workspace = true`.
